Ten for Teaching: Instituting flexible course policies that support all learners (ASYNCHRONOUS)

Boise State University Events

During the COVID-19 pandemic many educators loosened their course policies (e.g., around attendance and late work). Several years later, some of that flexibility has remained, with educators noting both positive and negative impacts on student learning. This dichotomy leads many of us to wonder what the right balance of flexibility is. In this workshop, we will begin by exploring the demographics of Boise State students and how those might impact the choices we make. Integrative Biology Seminar - Kathleen Hunt, Associate Professor

Oregon State University Events

Whales in Wartime: Retrospective assessment of stress physiology of large whales during 9/11 and World War II How are wildlife affected by chronic disturbances that never cease? From constant vessel traffic to widespread pollutants to relentless climate change, the natural environment today is full of anthropogenic disturbances that have become increasingly pervasive and continuous. The impacts of these "sub-lethal" disturbances on wildlife can be difficult to evaluate when there are no remaining un-exposed control groups to compare to. Is it even a bug? Whose bug is it anyway? What LLMs mistakes reveal about classifying software issue reports

UBC Okanagan Events

About the talk Your build breaks after a routine dependency update. Is that a bug? If so, whose bug is it, and where did it come from? Developers answer these questions every day when triaging issue reports, and getting them wrong can quietly contaminate the software bug datasets that much of software engineering research relies on. Prior studies have found that roughly one-third of reports labelled as bugs are not bugs at all. Large language models (LLMs) seem like a natural fit for automating this triage process. QPR Training – Saving Lives in Agriculture (in English)

Oregon State University Events

QPR ( Q uestion, P ersuade, R efer) is an evidence-based suicide prevention program where participants are empowered to make a positive difference in the lives of others. Similar to CPR, QPR provides lifesaving knowledge and skills to help someone in crisis. One myth about suicide is that once a person decides to commit suicide, there is nothing anyone can do to stop them. The fact is, suicide is the most preventable kind of death, and almost any positive action may save a life. Who should be trained in QPR to prevent farmer and rancher suicide? Those who know, love, and care for them: family and friends Medical providers, including dentists Bankers or financial counselors Veterinarians Farm
